questions.stem: Which two of these are Git providers that Fabric Git integration supports? Each correct answer is a complete solution.

options.text: Subversion
Azure DevOps
GitHub
Team Foundation Version Control
Mercurial

questions.explanation: Fabric Git integration works with Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitHub Enterprise (cloud-based).

questions.stem: How many Git branches can one Fabric workspace be connected to at a time?

options.text: One branch, and one folder in it
None; Git connects to items, not workspaces
Every branch in the repository
Up to three branches

questions.explanation: A workspace connects to one branch and one folder at a time. Developers who need another branch use another workspace.

questions.stem: A teammate committed changes to the branch your workspace is connected to. How do you bring them into the workspace?

options.text: Delete the workspace's items and recreate them
Run a deployment pipeline
Commit your workspace again
Use Update in the workspace's source control panel

questions.explanation: Commit sends workspace changes to Git; Update brings changes from the branch into the workspace.

questions.stem: Several developers work on features at once. In the development process Fabric documents, how do they avoid affecting each other and the shared Dev workspace?

options.text: Each developer copies items by hand into a personal workspace with no Git connection
Everyone edits the shared workspace and undoes mistakes later
Each developer works in their own workspace connected to their own separate branch
The shared workspace is disconnected from Git while anyone works

questions.explanation: Because a workspace connects to a single branch, each developer gets their own workspace on their own branch and merges through pull requests into the shared branch.

questions.stem: You connect a workspace that already holds finished items to a Git branch that also has content. You want to keep the workspace's items. Which sync direction do you choose?

options.text: Disconnect and reconnect until the branch is empty
Commit the workspace to the Git branch
Run a deployment pipeline into the workspace
Update the workspace from Git

questions.explanation: Committing exports the workspace's supported content to Git and overwrites the branch. Updating from Git would overwrite the workspace and lose its content.

questions.stem: You edited a notebook in a Git-connected workspace, but Commit is disabled. A teammate merged changes into the connected branch, and none touched your notebook. What do you do first?

options.text: Switch the workspace to a new branch
Disconnect the workspace from Git
Undo your notebook changes
Update the workspace from Git, then commit

questions.explanation: When the branch has updates, commits are disabled until you update the workspace. Your notebook isn't in conflict, so after the update you can commit it.

questions.stem: Which two statements about Commit and Update in Fabric Git integration are true? Each correct answer is a complete solution.

options.text: You can commit and update in one operation
You can choose which items to update from Git
Update keeps workspace changes on items that changed in both places
When several items changed, you can choose which ones to commit
Update always applies the whole branch, up to the latest commit

questions.explanation: Commit lets you pick items, but Update always brings in the entire branch. You can sync only one direction at a time, and items changed in both places are conflicts that block updates.

questions.stem: A notebook was changed in both the workspace and the Git branch. You resolve the conflict in the source control panel and choose Keep current content. What is the notebook's Git status afterwards?

options.text: Uncommitted changes
Update required
Synced
Unsupported item

questions.explanation: Keeping current content leaves the workspace version in place, which isn't in the branch yet, so its status becomes uncommitted changes. Accept incoming changes would make it synced.

questions.stem: A lead engineer has the Member role in a workspace and must connect it to an Azure DevOps repository. What is the least change that lets them do it?

options.text: Give them the Admin role in the workspace
Give them Contribute permission in the repository only
Give them Reshare permission on every item
Make them a pipeline admin

questions.explanation: Connecting a workspace to a Git repository requires the workspace Admin role. Members and Contributors can commit and update but can't connect.

questions.stem: A conflict can't be resolved in the Fabric UI, so you resolve it in Git. Put the steps in order.

options.text: In Git, resolve the conflicts between the original branch and the new branch
In Fabric, switch the workspace back to the original branch
Commit your changes into the new branch
In Git, merge the new branch into the original branch
From the Source control panel, check out a new branch from the last synced branch ID

questions.explanation: You branch from the last synced state, commit your work there, resolve and merge in Git, and then point the workspace back at the original branch.
